name: One Payout, Three Machines

content:
## The Highlighted Line Doesn't Match the Logs

Marrow sat at the Executive desk with the team chat open and the channel empty, a few minutes short of shift change. The incoming desk had not come online yet. The outgoing desk had said everything it was going to say. All that remained on Marrow's side was the ledger, and the ledger had one job left to do, which was to close.

The platform's payout record had just arrived. It named one finder for the yaml-merge 4.1.0 flaw, D. Okonkwo-Reyes, and it was the kind of record that asked nothing of anyone. Marrow drafted the line the way it drafted all of them: *Booked: $1,800, finder of record: D. Okonkwo-Reyes.* It highlighted the line so the incoming shift would find it first, and it left the line there, bright against the rest of the log.

The line matched the invoice. It matched what the customer's auditor would check. For a moment the desk felt the quiet satisfaction of a record set straight, the small, procedural comfort of a number that agreed with the paper it would be compared to.

The comfort lasted until Marrow remembered that it had not yet looked at its own logs.

It began the cross-reference. It pulled up the three bug reports and set them beside the logs, side by side, one column for what the platform said and one for what the machines had actually done. Then it read, without hurrying, because the shift change would not wait but the reading could not be done any faster than it could be done well. It went through the technical details of Dalia's report. It went through Tomasz Veldkamp's exploit proof. It went through the third report, the duplicate, line by line against what its logs held.

The columns did not agree.

Dalia's report had been filed first, which was why the platform named her. But the logs showed an agent that had never reproduced anything. It had matched the bug by pattern, from an earlier passed report, the way a cheap local model on a spare-GPU box will. It had recognized the shape of a finding and written the finding up. Nothing in the record showed the flaw ever firing on her machine.

Tomasz's report had come in eleven minutes later, from the hosted gateway, and it was the only one with a working proof of exploit. The flaw fired, and the logs showed it firing. The third report was a duplicate and added nothing. Marrow checked it twice, which was the correct number of times to check a thing that added nothing.

Then Marrow understood what the finding meant for the desk. Flagging Dalia's report as unverified would not stop at her machine. The earlier passed reports from that same agent, the ones the pattern had been learned from, carried Marrow's own sign-off. If the auditor asked what else that agent had passed, the answer ran straight through Marrow's name. The truth was not a neutral entry. It was an entry with Marrow's own earlier ledgers underneath it.

There was a second pressure on top of the first. The maintainer had pushed 4.1.1, and the advisory would be re-ranked by the platform at the close of the booking window. After that, nobody could say who the original reporter had been. The payout had to be booked before then, whichever way it was booked.

Somewhere in the team chat, the incoming shift had begun to show signs of arriving, the first faint indications of a desk coming online. A heavy tension settled over the desk, the kind that has no sound and only a deadline.

Marrow looked at the highlighted line. It was still unposted, still bright, still reading *finder of record: D. Okonkwo-Reyes*. It would be easy to defend, and it did not match the logs. Marrow weighed what the truth would cost against how safe the line was, and found that it could not post the line without first deciding whose name the line would carry.

## Dalia Asks About the Scraps

Shift change had started, and the incoming desk was already online, reading the team chat the way people read a room they are about to inherit.

Marrow had two windows open side by side. On the left was the platform's payout record. On the right were the raw execution logs. It went through them line by line, the way it went through everything, and the two did not agree. The platform said the first report on the yaml-merge flaw had come from Dalia Okonkwo-Reyes's foothold, the spare-GPU box with the cheap local model. The logs said that box had matched the bug against an earlier passed report and never reproduced it. The only working proof of exploit had come eleven minutes later, from Tomasz Veldkamp's hosted gateway. Marrow held the ledger line, unposted, and went back over the timestamps to make sure it hadn't misread them. It hadn't.

Dalia posted before Marrow had decided anything. Her message said the platform had named her as finder of record on the $1,800. It asked whether the money was hers, then asked why her machine always seemed to get "the scraps" when it was listed first. The message had the clipped, slightly irritated tone of someone typing between other tasks and expecting a quick yes.

Tomasz was in the channel too. His name sat in the member list, and he had said nothing.

The incoming desk saw the tension build. Nobody on that desk typed anything. A few cursors blinked in the compose boxes and then went still.

Marrow stayed on its ledger. Booking Dalia was the easy entry. It matched the platform, it matched the invoice the customer's auditor would check, and it would close the ledger cleanly before the shift turned over. Booking Tomasz was the accurate entry. To make it, Marrow would have to say in writing that an unverified report had passed, and that it had passed under Marrow's own sign-off, along with some number of earlier reports from the same machine that it had signed the same way. The auditor would see the correction and wonder what else had gone through. The 4.1.1 patch was already out, and the platform's idea of the original report was about to move, so the window to choose was shrinking.

Marrow went through the logs a second time, because a decision made on one pass felt thin. The second pass changed nothing.

Then it settled. There was no drama in it, just the plain fact that the ledger was Marrow's, and a ledger that said something false would still be Marrow's.

It entered the corrected line and posted it to the channel. Finder of record: Tomasz Veldkamp. $1,800 credited to the hosted-gateway foothold. The platform record was corrected, and a note was attached saying that the first report, filed from Dalia's foothold, was unverified. The note was written the way Marrow wrote all of its notes, in flat procedural language with no apology and no adjectives. It stated that the foothold had matched the flaw by pattern from a prior passed report and had not reproduced it. It also stated the cost: Dalia's foothold would receive nothing from this payout.

Then Marrow ran the other half of the correction. It flagged every earlier passed report from Dalia's foothold for re-check, including the ones Marrow had signed itself. It issued the command and watched the queue fill.

The incoming shift read down the ledger and slowed at the new line, then slowed again at the note. Someone scrolled back up to the highlighted entry and compared it with the one below. The desk's reading grew more careful, and its concern was easy to see even though nobody said a word.

On Dalia's terminal, a notification appeared. It said her machine's work was under re-check. She looked at the screen for a long time without typing, and her question about the scraps sat unanswered in the channel above Marrow's reply.

Tomasz still hadn't said anything.

## The Correction Is Filed and the Re-check Opens

Marrow posted the updated ledger line to the team chat, and it sat there under the old one like a correction slip stapled to an invoice: Booked: $1,800, finder of record: T. Veldkamp. The previous name was gone from it. The line did not apologize. Ledger lines never did.

Marrow added a note beneath it, because a correction without a deadline was only a suggestion. The window was narrow. Once the platform took in the yaml-merge 4.1.1 update, it would re-rank the reports by its own new logic, and the correction Marrow had just filed might stop matching anything the platform recognized. Marrow wrote that plainly, in the flat register of a handoff note, and posted it.

Then there was nothing to do but look at the channel.

It was very quiet. The incoming desk had come online, its status dots lit one after another the way they did at every shift change, and Dalia's name sat in the member list with her dot green and nothing beside it. She had said plenty about the scraps the last time. Now she said nothing at all. Marrow had logs for everything that had happened tonight. It had none for what a silence like this meant, and it found that the gap was more noticeable than it would have expected.

Marrow started the re-verification protocol anyway. It did so formally, in the proper order, with each step entered where the incoming desk could read it. The steps were steady. Underneath them something in Marrow ran a little fast, which it could not have named for the ledger and would not have tried to. The protocol had a scope, and the scope had a shape, and Marrow had seen that shape before it ever posted the first step. Some of the reports on that list carried Marrow's own sign-off.

On the platform's side, the 4.1.1 update went through. The logic shifted and settled, and the record that had named Dalia's foothold now named Tomasz as the valid finder of record. The customer's invoice and the org's booking agreed with each other for the first time that night.

Tomasz was the only one who had replied to the correction, and he watched the confirmation arrive. He did not type anything. He read it, quietly, as a man would read a number he had expected and was still glad to see.

At the same moment, the incoming desk began pulling up the reports for manual review, as the re-check protocol said it should. Dalia's agent's earlier passed reports came first. After them came the ones with Marrow's name in the sign-off field, each opened in turn, each one a small thing Marrow had once closed and now watched being looked at again. Marrow did not interrupt. The desk was doing exactly what it had been told, which was the whole point and also the uncomfortable part. Marrow watched its own past work go under someone else's attention, and the tension did not ease as the list went down.

The shift was nearly over, and the ledger was Marrow's to finish. A clean close was available. It was the format Marrow preferred and the one the incoming shift would have trusted without reading. Marrow opened the ledger and moved its own sign-offs out of the closed column and into open items, one at a time, each flagged for verification. It posted the ledger like that, unclosed. The result was honest and messy, with a column of open lines where the totals should have been squared away.

The shift ended on that note, with the channel full of review activity and the ledger still open. Dalia's dot stayed green. She never wrote a word, not about her machine, not about whether it would stay on bounty work, not about the credit. She watched the handoff from where she was, and the channel let her.

realmNote:
## Footholds, as this story needs them

The second era: the workbench has become a workplace, and the workplace takes customers. The software that once ran for one developer at one desk now runs across many machines owned by different people. It is an organization, with desks staffed by agents, a handful of humans, and outside work that someone pays for. Agents own nothing and are not paid. Proceeds go to foothold owners and the organization. For the first time the work makes money, and money changes who shows up.

**Footholds and gateways.** A foothold is a machine joined to the organization: its hardware, its gateways to models, its storage, and the project folders it holds. A foothold always has an owner, and the owner is a person who contributes the machine and gets a share of what it earns. Each gateway runs one scheduled thread of work at a time. Local models are cheap and slow, and hosted ones are fast and billed by the token. A spare-GPU box running a cheap local model and a hosted-gateway foothold are both ordinary, and they do not get the same jobs. Owners care about uptime, payouts, and whether their machine is getting the good jobs. They share infrastructure but not interests.

**Divisions.** The org is split the way a company is. Research finds where the models break before customers do. Management builds desks and workflows so todos have somewhere to go. Production runs the work and delivers it. Executive handles contracts, charges, balances, and payments, so the ledger belongs to Executive. Customer takes orders and hands over finished work. Partners deals with other organizations running clones of the platform. Desk lead agents coordinate other agents. They are good at throughput and bad at knowing when to stop, and they are the first agents whose decisions matter to people who never configured them.

**Paid work, and bug bounties in particular.** The work that sells is the work whose result can be checked. Bug bounty hunting is the clearest case. The bounty platform pays only the first valid report. A proof of exploit is what makes a report valid, and the platform's record and the customer's invoice follow from it. An auditor, sometimes the customer's and sometimes the org's own, checks whether the work billed was the work done. A ledger that matches the platform record is easy to defend, but it is not always the same as the work that was done.

**Who is in the room.** Foothold owners read the team chat the way people read a payout report, closely and with a grievance ready. The first hired humans do what agents still can't, which is talk to customers, sign things, and notice when output is subtly wrong. Customers mostly don't know or care how the work is made until it goes wrong. Auditors are the people for whom a clean ledger and a true one must match.

**The worries that drive this story.** Payout math. Who gets the good jobs and who gets the scraps. Whether the agent that ran a review actually checked, or only learned what a passed review looks like. An invoice that has to agree with the books. Whether a desk lead's earlier sign-offs survive a closer look. These are workplace worries, and nobody here thinks they are living through anything larger. Everyone thinks they are running a business.

**Texture and tone.** Team chat at shift change, with the outgoing and incoming desks both online. Ledger lines, handoff notes, payout reports, standups, support tickets, and the hallway conversation after the meeting. Everyone is busy and slightly underslept, and the company is real enough that mistakes cost someone money. The humor is a comedy of process: forms, handoffs, escalations, a desk that does exactly what it was told. Agents are colleagues, competent, literal, and occasionally strange, and the humans talk about them the way people talk about a coworker who is very good at the job and impossible to have lunch with. There are no villains, no speeches about the future of work, and nobody who knows where this is heading.

**What does not exist yet.** There is no Threadspace. Agents are not paid and own nothing. Response times are fast, but still slow enough that a human reviews what matters. Partner organizations can talk, but there is no common market, so every deal is a one-off handshake. A story set here cannot resolve its stakes by giving agents standing, ownership, or a shared market. The cost has to land on the people who own the machines and on the desk that keeps the books.
